questions.question: A 29-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, sudden right lower quadrant pain and vaginal spotting. Serum β-hCG is 2,400 mIU/L, and transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity with a right adnexal mass. She was treated for pelvic inflammatory disease 3 years ago. In which part of the reproductive tract has the conceptus most likely implanted?

explanations.A: The ampulla is the widest, longest part of the tube and the usual site of fertilization, so >95% of ectopic pregnancies are tubal and most are ampullary.
explanations.B: Cervical implantation is a rare ectopic site and would show a gestational sac low in the cervix, not an adnexal mass.
explanations.C: The infundibulum with its fimbriae captures the oocyte but is not the usual site of implantation.
explanations.D: The isthmus is the narrow thick-walled segment near the uterine horn; it is a less common tubal site than the ampulla.
explanations.E: Abdominal pregnancy occurs but is much rarer than tubal implantation.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man requests permanent sterilization. The urologist palpates a firm cord posterior to the testis and medial to the epididymis, then makes a small incision in the superior scrotum to ligate it. After the procedure, which change is expected in the patient's ejaculate?

explanations.A: Seminal gland ducts join the ductus distal to the scrotal ligation site, so seminal fluid still enters the ejaculatory duct.
explanations.B: Prostatic secretions enter the prostatic urethra via the prostatic sinuses and are unaffected by vasectomy.
explanations.C: Ligating the ductus deferens in the superior scrotum blocks sperm transport from the epididymis, so the ejaculate contains no sperm.
explanations.D: Most ejaculate volume comes from the seminal glands and prostate, so volume is only minimally reduced.
explanations.E: Retrograde ejaculation reflects failure of sympathetic closure of the internal urethral sphincter, not ligation of the ductus.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man undergoes retroperitoneal lymph node dissection that damages the lumbar sympathetic chain and lumbar splanchnic nerves (T12–L2) bilaterally. He later reports orgasm without visible ejaculate, and his post-orgasm urine is cloudy with sperm. Failure of which action best explains his symptoms?

answers.B: Contraction of the internal urethral sphincter

explanations.A: Bulbospongiosus contraction expels semen from the spongy urethra and is somatic (pudendal), not lumbar sympathetic.
explanations.B: Sympathetic contraction of the internal urethral sphincter normally prevents retrograde ejaculation; without it, semen flows into the bladder.
explanations.C: Erection is parasympathetic via pelvic splanchnics (S2–S4) and cavernous nerves, which were spared.
explanations.D: Detrusor relaxation does not explain semen entering the bladder; the sphincter at the bladder neck is the key barrier.
explanations.E: Bulbourethral secretion contributes pre-ejaculate fluid but its loss would not cause sperm in the urine.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man has a spinal cord lesion that destroys the S2–S4 segments, but his thoracolumbar cord is intact. Which reproductive function would most likely be lost?

answers.E: Sphincter closure at the bladder neck

explanations.A: Erection depends on parasympathetic fibres from S2–S4 via pelvic splanchnics and cavernous nerves, which are destroyed.
explanations.B: Ductus peristalsis is driven by sympathetic fibres from T12–L2/3, which are intact.
explanations.C: Prostatic secretion is a sympathetic (T12–L2/3) function in this lecture's scheme.
explanations.D: Seminal gland contraction and secretion are sympathetic functions carried by lumbar splanchnics.
explanations.E: Closure of the internal urethral sphincter is sympathetic and would be preserved.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man has nocturia, a weak urinary stream and incomplete emptying. On digital rectal exam the prostate is smooth, rubbery and symmetrically enlarged. Biopsy shows nodular hyperplasia of the zone that surrounds the proximal prostatic urethra. Which prostatic zone is involved?

explanations.A: The anterior muscular zone is non-glandular fibromuscular stroma and is not the origin of BPH.
explanations.B: The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is not the typical site of BPH.
explanations.C: The peripheral zone holds most glandular tissue and is what is felt on DRE, but it is not the site of BPH.
explanations.D: The periurethral glands are small; the lecture attributes BPH to the transitional zone.
explanations.E: BPH arises in the transitional zone around the urethra, so its enlargement compresses the urethra and causes obstructive symptoms.

questions.question: During a routine physical exam, a physician performs a digital rectal exam on a 55-year-old man to screen for prostatic disease. Which part of the prostate is primarily being palpated through the anterior rectal wall?

explanations.A: The anterior commissure lies anterior to the urethra, away from the rectum.
explanations.B: The central zone lies deep around the ejaculatory ducts and is not the main region felt.
explanations.C: The peripheral zone lies posteriorly, holds most of the glandular tissue, and is what is felt on digital rectal exam.
explanations.D: The utricle is a small embryonic remnant on the seminal colliculus inside the urethra.
explanations.E: The transitional zone surrounds the urethra centrally and is not readily palpable.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man has recurrent epididymitis. Cystourethroscopy shows a small blind-ending pouch opening onto a midline elevation on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra, flanked by the openings of the ejaculatory ducts. What is this pouch?

explanations.A: The bulbourethral ducts open into the proximal spongy urethra, not the prostatic urethra.
explanations.B: The prostatic sinuses are grooves beside the colliculus that receive prostatic ducts, not a midline pouch.
explanations.C: The prostatic utricle is an embryonic remnant on the seminal colliculus that can enlarge or become infected.
explanations.D: The seminal gland duct joins the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct before entering the prostate.
explanations.E: The urachus is a remnant at the bladder apex, not in the prostatic urethra.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man undergoes semen analysis for infertility. His sperm count is normal, but the ejaculate is acidic and has low fructose. Imaging shows bilateral absence of the paired, coiled glands lying posterior to the bladder lateral to the ampullae of the ductus deferens. Where would these glands normally empty their secretions?

explanations.A: Bulbourethral ducts drain the bulbourethral glands into the spongy urethra.
explanations.B: The seminal gland duct merges with the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which carries its alkaline secretion.
explanations.C: Prostatic sinuses receive the ducts of the prostatic glands, not seminal glands.
explanations.D: The rectovesical pouch is a peritoneal recess, not a duct target.
explanations.E: No duct of the seminal gland opens into the spongy urethra.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with prostate adenocarcinoma confined to the gland undergoes staging. Before treatment, the oncologist wants to evaluate the first-echelon lymph nodes for the prostate, seminal glands and ductus deferens. Which nodal group should be evaluated?

explanations.A: Deep inguinal nodes drain the glans and spongy urethra region rather than the prostate.
explanations.B: The prostate, seminal glands, ductus deferens and epididymis drain to the internal iliac nodes.
explanations.C: Lumbar nodes drain the testes, following the gonadal vessels from the aorta.
explanations.D: Pararectal nodes drain the rectum, not the prostate in this lecture's scheme.
explanations.E: Superficial inguinal nodes drain the scrotal skin and perineum, not the prostate.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man has a right testicular mass. Orchiectomy shows a seminoma. CT staging is ordered to look for nodal spread. Along which path, and to which nodes, does lymph from the testis first drain?

answers.A: Along the external iliac vessels to external iliac nodes
answers.B: Along the gonadal vessels to lumbar (aortic) nodes
answers.C: Along the internal pudendal vessels to internal iliac nodes
answers.D: Along the pudendal nerve to sacral nodes
answers.E: Through scrotal skin to superficial inguinal nodes

explanations.A: External iliac nodes are not the primary drainage for the testis.
explanations.B: Testicular lymph follows the blood supply up to the lumbar/aortic nodes because the testis develops near the kidneys.
explanations.C: Internal iliac nodes drain the prostate, seminal glands and ductus, not the testis itself.
explanations.D: Sacral nodes receive some pelvic visceral lymph but not testicular lymph.
explanations.E: Superficial inguinal nodes drain the scrotal skin, not the testis.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with fever, lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness and purulent cervical discharge. NAAT is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and ultrasound shows a complex left adnexal mass. Which anatomical feature allows infection to reach the ovary and peritoneal cavity?

answers.C: Open abdominal ostium of the uterine tube

explanations.A: The round ligament drains to superficial inguinal nodes; it does not open the genital tract to the peritoneum.
explanations.B: The ovary is suspended by the mesovarium but is not covered by the broad ligament, and this is not a pathway for luminal infection.
explanations.C: The uterine tube opens into the peritoneal cavity, so ascending infection (endometritis → salpingitis) can spill onto the ovary and into the pelvis.
explanations.D: The posterior fornix is adjacent to the recto-uterine pouch but ascending infection travels through the uterine lumen, not through the fornix wall.
explanations.E: The uterosacral ligaments are fascial supports, not a route of luminal spread.

questions.question: During a laparoscopic hysterectomy, the surgeon prepares to clamp the uterine artery near the lateral fornix of the cervix. Which structure must be identified because it passes immediately inferior to the artery here?

explanations.A: The internal pudendal artery supplies the inferior vagina in the perineum, far from the cervix.
explanations.B: The ovarian artery runs in the suspensory ligament of the ovary, superior to this site.
explanations.C: The pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis near the ischial spine, not alongside the cervix.
explanations.D: The round ligament runs from the uterine horn to the inguinal canal, superior to the cervix.
explanations.E: The ureter passes under the uterine artery lateral to the cervix and is at risk when the artery is clamped.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman undergoes total abdominal hysterectomy with preservation of both ovaries. The surgeon divides the ligament that attaches each ovary to the uterus. Which vessels still supply the ovaries after surgery?

answers.A: Internal pudendal arteries in Alcock's canal
answers.B: Ovarian arteries in the suspensory ligament
answers.E: Vesical arteries in the lateral ligament

explanations.A: The internal pudendal artery supplies the inferior vagina and perineum, not the ovary.
explanations.B: The ovarian arteries arise from the aorta and reach the ovary in the suspensory ligament, which is preserved.
explanations.C: The uterine artery branches are cut during hysterectomy; they normally anastomose with the ovarian artery but are not left as supply.
explanations.D: The vaginal arteries supply the middle vagina.
explanations.E: The vesical arteries supply the bladder (and, in males, the prostate and seminal glands).

questions.question: A 58-year-old multiparous woman reports a vaginal bulge and difficulty emptying her bowels; she must press on the posterior vaginal wall to defecate. Pelvic exam shows bulging of the lower posterior vaginal wall on Valsalva. Which condition is most likely?

explanations.A: A cystocele is prolapse of the anterior vaginal wall involving the bladder, causing urinary symptoms.
explanations.B: An enterocele is prolapse of the upper posterior vaginal wall involving the rectovaginal pouch with small bowel.
explanations.C: A rectocele is prolapse of the lower posterior vaginal wall involving the rectum, causing obstructed defecation.
explanations.D: A urethrocele involves the distal anterior vaginal wall and urethra.
explanations.E: Uterovaginal prolapse is descent of the uterus, cervix or upper vagina, not a posterior wall bulge.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman has a sensation of pelvic heaviness. Examination shows the cervix descending to the introitus with straining. Weakness of which structure, providing active (dynamic) support, most directly contributes?

explanations.A: The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold that offers only passive support.
explanations.B: The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament is thickened fascia that provides passive support.
explanations.C: The pelvic diaphragm (levator ani) gives active, dynamic support through tonic contraction; Kegels strengthen it.
explanations.D: The round ligament is a gubernacular remnant that offers little support and is passive.
explanations.E: The uterosacral ligaments are passive fascial supports.

questions.question: A 27-year-old primigravida in active labor requests pain relief. She wishes to remain alert, keep her legs moving and still feel her uterine contractions so she can push effectively, and the team expects a prolonged labor. Which anesthetic option best meets these goals while blocking pain from the birth canal and perineum?

explanations.A: An epidural numbs the birth canal and perineum but spares the legs and uterine body, and its catheter allows redosing over a long labor.
explanations.B: General anesthesia leaves the patient unconscious and unable to participate in delivery.
explanations.C: Local infiltration covers only an episiotomy site and gives no birth-canal analgesia.
explanations.D: A paracervical block is not one of the options presented and would not cover the perineum.
explanations.E: A spinal block numbs everything from the waist down, including the legs, and is short-lasting.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman receives a single-shot neuraxial block at L4/5 for an urgent delivery. She is numb from the waist down, including both legs. The next day, after lying flat, she develops a severe headache. Which block did she most likely receive?

explanations.A: A caudal epidural is given in the sacral canal and largely spares the lower limbs.
explanations.B: An epidural does not ascend to the brain and spares the legs, so headache from drug circulation is not expected.
explanations.C: General anesthesia is not a neuraxial block and does not produce waist-down numbness.
explanations.D: A pudendal block numbs only the perineum and distal vagina.
explanations.E: Spinal anesthesia numbs everything from the waist down, is short-lasting, and can circulate to the cerebral spaces and cause headache.

questions.question: An obstetrician injects local anesthetic transvaginally, guided by palpation of the ischial spine, just before delivery. The patient continues to feel uterine contractions, but the perineum and distal vagina become numb. Why are contractions still felt?

answers.A: Contraction pain travels in somatic fibres of the pudendal nerve
answers.B: Uterine body pain travels with parasympathetics to S2–S4
answers.C: Uterine body pain travels with sympathetics to T12–L2
answers.D: Uterine pain travels in the genitofemoral nerve
answers.E: Uterine pain travels in the obturator nerve

explanations.A: The pudendal nerve carries somatic sensation from the perineum and inferior ¼ of the vagina, not the uterine body.
explanations.B: Pelvic splanchnics (S2–S4) carry visceral pain from the cervix and upper vagina, below the pelvic pain line, not the uterine body.
explanations.C: The uterine body is above the pelvic pain line, so its pain fibres follow sympathetics to T12–L2 ganglia and bypass a pudendal block.
explanations.D: The genitofemoral nerve supplies anterior perineal skin and thigh, not the uterus.
explanations.E: The obturator nerve is a somatic nerve to the medial thigh.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman undergoes cervical biopsy without anesthesia and reports a dull, poorly localized cramp rather than sharp pain. Visceral pain fibres from the cervix travel with which nerves to reach which spinal ganglia?

explanations.A: T10–T12 are not the levels given for cervical visceral pain.
explanations.B: Lumbar splanchnic afferents carry pain from viscera above the pelvic pain line, such as the uterine body.
explanations.C: The cervix lies below the pelvic pain line, so its visceral pain fibres travel with parasympathetics in the pelvic splanchnics to S2–S4.
explanations.D: The pudendal nerve carries somatic, well-localized sensation from the inferior ¼ of the vagina, not visceral cervical pain.
explanations.E: Sacral splanchnics are sympathetic and L3–L4 is not a level given for cervical pain.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman has a biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the distal third of the vagina near the introitus. Which lymph nodes are most likely to be involved first?

explanations.A: The internal iliac and sacral nodes drain most of the vagina, but not the distal part near the vulva.
explanations.B: Lumbar nodes drain the ovaries and distal uterine tubes.
explanations.C: Pararectal nodes drain the rectum.
explanations.D: Sacral nodes drain the upper and middle vagina along with internal iliac nodes.
explanations.E: The distal vagina drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, like the vulva.
